description: PPA L0-L3 concept graph. 'altitude' is the concept's home altitude (architecture/ARCHITECTURE.md §3): L0 = routing/orientation discriminators; L1 = stated with all side conditions in an L1 reference; L2 = actionable procedures; L3 = formal detail consulted via corpus shards or ontology indices. Units 0-2: Appendices A-C, Index of Notation, Chapter 1, and Chapter 2. Terms marked [external] are outside the book.

concepts.title: Partial ordering and partially ordered set
concepts.formal_summary: A partial ordering ⊑ on L is reflexive, transitive and anti-symmetric; (L, ⊑) is a partially ordered set. l₁ ⊏ l₂ means l₁ ⊑ l₂ ∧ l₁ ≠ l₂.

projections.cs_theory: Base structure for every property space in the book; ⊑ reads 'is more precise than'.
projections.swe_architecture: Any merge-able analysis state needs an explicit, documented order before transfer functions are written.
projections.practical_debugging: If two states compare both ways but differ, anti-symmetry is violated: the encoding is not canonical.
projections.cyber: Security labels and taint states [external] must form a partial order whose direction (may vs must) is stated up front.

concepts.title: Upper and lower bounds, least upper bound (join) and greatest lower bound (meet)
concepts.formal_summary: For Y ⊆ L, ⨆Y is an upper bound below every upper bound and ⨅Y a lower bound above every lower bound; they need not exist and are unique when they exist. l₁ ⊔ l₂ = ⨆{l₁, l₂}, l₁ ⊓ l₂ = ⨅{l₁, l₂}.

projections.cs_theory: Join combines information at control-flow merges; existence is not automatic in an arbitrary poset.
projections.swe_architecture: A merge operator must be the least upper bound, not just some upper bound, or precision is silently lost.
projections.practical_debugging: Merges that are not idempotent, commutative and associative indicate the join is not a lub.
projections.cyber: Choosing ∪ vs ∩ as the join encodes may vs must semantics; the wrong choice yields false security.

concepts.title: Complete lattice
concepts.formal_summary: A partially ordered set in which all subsets have least upper bounds and greatest lower bounds; ⊥ = ⨆∅ = ⨅L and ⊤ = ⨅∅ = ⨆L.

projections.cs_theory: Guarantees that lfp and gfp of monotone maps exist (Proposition A.10).
projections.swe_architecture: Property spaces are designed as complete lattices so least solutions exist regardless of program shape.
projections.practical_debugging: A missing ⊤ or ⊥ (e.g. no value for 'unknown') breaks completeness and makes the solver's start state ill-defined.
projections.cyber: Security lattices need explicit top and bottom elements; partial label sets without bounds cannot be solved soundly.

concepts.title: Powerset lattices (𝒫(S), ⊆) and (𝒫(S), ⊇)
concepts.formal_summary: (𝒫(S), ⊆) has ⨆ = ⋃, ⨅ = ⋂, ⊥ = ∅, ⊤ = S; (𝒫(S), ⊇) is its dual with ⨆ = ⋂, ⨅ = ⋃, ⊥ = S, ⊤ = ∅ (Example A.1). Both are complete lattices.

projections.cs_theory: The two classical property spaces of bit-vector analyses; duality swaps may and must.
projections.swe_architecture: Bit-vector implementations realise these lattices directly; the order direction chooses union or intersection at merges.
projections.practical_debugging: A must-analysis initialised with ∅ instead of S converges to a wrong, too-small result.
projections.cyber: Taint (may, ⊆) and sanitizer dominance (must, ⊇) [external] use the two dual powerset lattices.

concepts.title: Lemma A.2: complete lattice from one-sided bounds
concepts.formal_summary: For a partially ordered set the following are equivalent: (i) it is a complete lattice; (ii) every subset has a least upper bound; (iii) every subset has a greatest lower bound.

projections.cs_theory: Completeness can be checked on joins alone; meets are then definable by (A.1).
projections.swe_architecture: A lattice library only needs a correct arbitrary join; meet can be derived.
projections.practical_debugging: If arbitrary joins exist but meets are hand-written inconsistently, derive meet from join to remove the mismatch.
projections.cyber: Label lattices defined by a join table alone are complete when every subset has a join.

concepts.title: Moore family
concepts.formal_summary: Y ⊆ L (L a complete lattice) is a Moore family iff ∀Y′ ⊆ Y : ⨅Y′ ∈ Y; it contains ⨅Y and ⨅∅ = ⊤, so it is never empty (Example A.3).

projections.cs_theory: Closure under arbitrary meets is what makes least acceptable analysis results exist (used in Chapter 3).
projections.swe_architecture: A set of acceptable solutions closed under meet has a unique best element that a solver can target.
projections.practical_debugging: If the set of valid results is empty or not closed under ⊓, there is no least solution to report.
projections.cyber: A policy family must contain ⊤ and be meet-closed for a least-privilege [external] solution to exist.

concepts.title: Properties of functions between partially ordered sets
concepts.formal_summary: f : L₁ → L₂ may be surjective, injective, monotone (l ⊑ l′ ⇒ f(l) ⊑ f(l′)), additive (preserves binary ⊔; also called distributive), multiplicative, completely additive or multiplicative (preserves ⨆/⨅ of all Y when defined), affine (preserves ⨆ of non-empty Y) or strict (f(⊥) = ⊥). Completely additive iff affine and strict.

projections.cs_theory: Monotonicity is the precondition of Proposition A.10; additivity governs precision (MFP vs MOP in Chapter 2).
projections.swe_architecture: Transfer functions should be written in a form whose monotonicity is evident (e.g. gen/kill).
projections.practical_debugging: Order-dependent results or oscillation in a solver point to a non-monotone transfer function.
projections.cyber: Non-monotone constructs (e.g. negation inside recursive rules, declassification [external]) break least-fixed-point reasoning.

concepts.title: Lemma A.4: complete multiplicativity on a finite domain
concepts.formal_summary: For complete lattices L and M with M finite, γ : M → L is completely multiplicative iff (i) γ is monotone, (ii) γ(⊤) = ⊤, and (iii) γ(m₁ ⊓ m₂) = γ(m₁) ⊓ γ(m₂) whenever m₁ and m₂ are incomparable.

projections.cs_theory: Reduces an infinitary preservation property to finitely many checks when M is finite.
projections.swe_architecture: A finite abstract domain's concretisation can be validated by checking ⊤ and incomparable pairs only.
projections.practical_debugging: The finiteness of M is essential; the shortcut is unsound for infinite domains.
projections.cyber: Finite label domains can have their meaning maps verified exhaustively with this lemma.

concepts.title: Lemma A.5: affine and completely additive maps between powersets
concepts.formal_summary: f : (𝒫(D), ⊆) → (𝒫(E), ⊆) is affine iff f(Y) = ⋃{φ(d) | d ∈ Y} ∪ φ_∅ for some φ : D → 𝒫(E) and φ_∅ ∈ 𝒫(E); it is completely additive iff additionally φ_∅ = ∅.

projections.cs_theory: Characterises the transfer functions of bit-vector frameworks by pointwise generators.
projections.swe_architecture: Per-element generator tables give a compact, verifiable encoding of transfer functions.
projections.practical_debugging: A transfer function that cannot be written in this form is not affine; expect precision loss at merges.
projections.cyber: Taint propagation rules [external] expressed as per-source generator sets are affine by construction.

concepts.title: Isomorphism of partially ordered sets
concepts.formal_summary: θ : L₁ → L₂ is an isomorphism if it is monotone and has a (necessarily unique) monotone inverse θ⁻¹ with θ ∘ θ⁻¹ = id₂ and θ⁻¹ ∘ θ = id₁.

projections.cs_theory: Isomorphic property spaces support identical analyses.
projections.swe_architecture: Changing representation (e.g. bit vector vs sorted set) is safe when it is an order isomorphism.
projections.practical_debugging: A representation change that is a bijection but not monotone both ways silently changes results.
projections.cyber: Label encodings may be swapped only through order isomorphisms.

concepts.title: Constructions of complete lattices: cartesian product, total and monotone function spaces
concepts.formal_summary: L₁ × L₂ ordered componentwise; S → L₁ (total functions, pointwise order); L₁ → L₂ (monotone functions, pointwise order). Each is a complete lattice when its components are, with joins, meets, ⊥ and ⊤ computed componentwise or pointwise.

projections.cs_theory: Compound property spaces inherit completeness from their parts.
projections.swe_architecture: Analysis states such as 'map from variables to abstract values' are total function spaces; per-component code reuse follows.
projections.practical_debugging: Pointwise joins that are not computed per key indicate a broken map-lattice implementation.
projections.cyber: Per-variable or per-object security state is a function space over a label lattice.

concepts.title: Smash product
concepts.formal_summary: The variant of the cartesian product restricted to pairs (l₁, l₂) with l₁ = ⊥₁ ⇔ l₂ = ⊥₂.

projections.cs_theory: Identifies all pairs containing a bottom component with (⊥, ⊥).
projections.swe_architecture: Useful when a bottom component means the whole state is unreachable.
projections.practical_debugging: Using a plain product where a smash product is intended keeps meaningless half-bottom states alive.
projections.cyber: Collapsing unreachable-branch states avoids reporting findings on dead paths.

concepts.title: Chains, ascending and descending chains, eventual stabilisation
concepts.formal_summary: Y ⊆ L is a chain if any two elements are comparable. A sequence (lₙ)ₙ is ascending if n ≤ m ⇒ lₙ ⊑ lₘ, descending if n ≤ m ⇒ lₙ ⊒ lₘ, and eventually stabilises iff ∃n₀ : ∀n ≥ n₀ : lₙ = l_{n₀}.

projections.cs_theory: Fixed-point iteration from ⊥ produces an ascending chain.
projections.swe_architecture: Solver termination arguments are statements about chains of states per program point.
projections.practical_debugging: A per-point value that keeps growing without stabilising is an ascending chain that does not stabilise.
projections.cyber: Unbounded growth in analyser state is a resource-exhaustion risk.

concepts.title: Finite height, Ascending and Descending Chain Conditions
concepts.formal_summary: L has finite height iff all chains are finite; ACC iff every ascending chain eventually stabilises; DCC iff every descending chain does. Lemma A.6: finite height ⇔ ACC ∧ DCC. Example A.7: ACC (or DCC) alone does not imply finite height.

projections.cs_theory: ACC is the termination condition for iteration from ⊥; finite height is strictly stronger.
projections.swe_architecture: Choose finite-height or ACC domains, or provide widening (Chapter 4), before promising termination.
projections.practical_debugging: Non-termination of a worklist solver indicates an infinite ascending chain in the domain; check ACC first.
projections.cyber: Analysers over domains without ACC can be driven into non-termination by crafted inputs.

concepts.title: Preservation of chain conditions by constructions
concepts.formal_summary: Finite height, ACC and DCC are preserved by L₁ × L₂; the total function space S → L preserves them only when S is finite; the monotone function space does not preserve them in general.

projections.cs_theory: Termination of compound domains depends on the finiteness of their index sets.
projections.swe_architecture: Maps keyed by an unbounded key set (heap addresses, call strings) lose ACC even if the value lattice has it.
projections.practical_debugging: Termination that holds on small tests but fails at scale often comes from an unbounded map domain.
projections.cyber: Attacker-controlled key growth (e.g. dynamic object creation) can defeat ACC of map-based states.

concepts.title: Lemma A.8: ACC complete lattices from ⊥ and binary joins
concepts.formal_summary: A partially ordered set is a complete lattice satisfying ACC iff it has a least element, binary least upper bounds, and satisfies ACC.

projections.cs_theory: Under ACC, completeness reduces to ⊥ plus binary joins.
projections.swe_architecture: A domain implementation with bottom, binary join and ACC needs no infinitary join operation.
projections.practical_debugging: Missing bottom is the usual reason such a domain fails to be a complete lattice.
projections.cyber: Finite label sets with bottom and pairwise join are complete lattices.

concepts.title: Lemma A.9: additive iff affine under ACC
concepts.formal_summary: For a complete lattice satisfying ACC and total f : L → L: f is additive iff f is affine; in both cases f is monotone.

projections.cs_theory: Under ACC on a complete lattice with total f : L → L, binary join preservation (additivity) suffices for preservation of all non-empty joins (affinity).
projections.swe_architecture: Checking pairwise distributivity of a transfer function is enough when the domain has ACC.
projections.practical_debugging: Without ACC, a function preserving binary joins may still fail on infinite joins.
projections.cyber: Under ACC, distributive (additive) security transfer functions preserve non-empty joins so merge-over-paths and fixed-point results align [external].

concepts.title: Fixed points, reductive and extensive sets, lfp and gfp
concepts.formal_summary: For monotone f on a complete lattice: Fix(f) = {l | f(l) = l}, Red(f) = {l | f(l) ⊑ l}, Ext(f) = {l | f(l) ⊒ l}, lfp(f) = ⨅Fix(f), gfp(f) = ⨆Fix(f).

projections.cs_theory: Analysis results are characterised as least (sometimes greatest) fixed points.
projections.swe_architecture: A candidate solution can be validated by one application of f: it is a fixed point, or at least reductive.
projections.practical_debugging: If f(l) ⋢ l for a reported result l, l is not reductive (l ∉ Red(f)) and is unsound for a least-fixed-point specification.
projections.cyber: Least fixed points model least privilege [external]; greatest fixed points give optimistic (coinductive) acceptance.

concepts.title: Proposition A.10: Tarski's Fixed Point Theorem
concepts.formal_summary: For a complete lattice L and monotone f : L → L: lfp(f) = ⨅Red(f) ∈ Fix(f) and gfp(f) = ⨆Ext(f) ∈ Fix(f); they are the least and greatest fixed points.

projections.cs_theory: Existence of least and greatest solutions for every monotone equation system over a complete lattice.
projections.swe_architecture: Equation-based analyses are well defined once domain completeness and transfer monotonicity are checked.
projections.practical_debugging: Both preconditions (complete lattice, monotone f) must be checked; existence says nothing about computability.
projections.cyber: Policy or type checkers defined by recursive monotone rules have well-defined least and greatest readings.

conditions: Monotone predicate functional 𝒬 on complete lattice (D → {true, false}, ⊑); rule form (B.5) agrees with Q = lfp(𝒬) when each rule makes finitely many recursive calls to Q
differs: Proposition A.10 characterises lfp(𝒬) = ⨅Red(𝒬) order-theoretically, whereas Appendix B presents inductive definitions as finitary inference rules (B.5) proved by rule-validity induction

conditions: Monotone predicate functional 𝒬 on complete lattice (D → {true, false}, ⊑) with coinductive specification Q = gfp(𝒬)
differs: Proposition A.10 gives the lattice identity gfp(𝒬) = ⨆Ext(𝒬), whereas §B.3 packages witness membership Q′ ∈ Ext(𝒬) (Q′ ⊑ 𝒬(Q′) or Q′ ⊑ 𝒬(Q ⊔ Q′)) as the coinduction proof principle

conditions: Positive monotone acceptability functional Q on complete predicate lattice ((Cache_hat x Env_hat x Exp) -> {true, false}, <=)
differs: Section 3.1.2 instantiates gfp(Q) on dynamic call acceptability |= while Proposition 3.16 proves lfp(Q) fails the Moore-family property on self-application, whereas Appendix B develops general coinduction over Appendix A.4 fixed points

concepts.title: Iteration towards fixed points and its bounds
concepts.formal_summary: For monotone f : L → L on a complete lattice L, in general ⊥ ⊑ fⁿ(⊥) ⊑ ⨆ₙ fⁿ(⊥) ⊑ lfp(f) ⊑ gfp(f) ⊑ ⨅ₙ fⁿ(⊤) ⊑ fⁿ(⊤) ⊑ ⊤ and each ⊑ can be strict. Under ACC, ∃n : fⁿ(⊥) = fⁿ⁺¹(⊥) = lfp(f); under DCC, ∃n : fⁿ(⊤) = fⁿ⁺¹(⊤) = gfp(f).

projections.cs_theory: Ascending iteration fⁿ(⊥) is guaranteed to stabilise at lfp(f) in finitely many steps under ACC, while continuity guarantees limit equality ⨆ₙ fⁿ(⊥) = lfp(f) (Kleene-style iteration [external]).
projections.swe_architecture: Start iteration at ⊥ for least solutions and stop at the first repeat; ACC is a sufficient condition for finite-step convergence to lfp(f).
projections.practical_debugging: A solver that 'converges' without ACC may stop below lfp (the limit need not be a fixed point).
projections.cyber: Starting from ⊤ computes a greatest fixed point: a different, optimistic answer.

concepts.title: Transfinite iteration
concepts.formal_summary: f^{↑κ} = f(⨆_{κ′<κ} f^{↑κ′}) for ordinals κ; for natural n, f^{↑n} = fⁿ⁺¹(⊥) (note the index offset); lfp(f) = f^{↑κ} for a cardinal κ greater than the cardinality of L.

projections.cs_theory: Without ACC or continuity, lfp is reached only after transfinitely many steps.
projections.swe_architecture: Explains why finite iteration is not a general algorithm on infinite-height domains.
projections.practical_debugging: Mind the index offset between f^{↑n} and fⁿ(⊥) when quoting iteration counts.
projections.cyber: Termination guarantees cannot be recovered from transfinite constructions; use widening.

concepts.title: Induction principles: mathematical, structural, on inference trees, course of values
concepts.formal_summary: Mathematical induction (Q(0), Q(n) ⇒ Q(n+1)); structural induction over d ::= Base | Con₁(d) | Con₂(d, d); induction on the shape of inference trees d →^▽ n; course of values induction ((∀m < n : Q(m)) ⇒ Q(n)).

projections.cs_theory: The proof principles behind the book's semantic correctness results.
projections.swe_architecture: Recursive processing of syntax trees mirrors structural induction; each constructor needs a case.
projections.practical_debugging: A recursive function missing a constructor case is a structural-induction proof with a missing case.
projections.cyber: Proofs that a sanitizer [external] is applied on every derivation are inductions on derivations.

concepts.title: Well-founded ordering and well-founded induction
concepts.formal_summary: ⪯ on D is well-founded if there is no infinite strictly decreasing sequence d₁ ≻ d₂ ≻ ⋯ (this amounts to the Descending Chain Condition); principle: from ∀d : (∀d′ ≺ d : Q(d′)) ⇒ Q(d) conclude ∀d : Q(d).

projections.cs_theory: Generalises course of values induction; termination proofs use well-founded measures.
projections.swe_architecture: Recursive algorithms terminate when each call decreases a well-founded measure.
projections.practical_debugging: Look for an infinite descending sequence of the measure to explain non-termination.
projections.cyber: Recursion over attacker-controlled structures needs a well-founded measure to bound work.

concepts.title: Predicates as fixed points of monotone functionals
concepts.formal_summary: Recursive predicate definitions Qᵢ = 𝒬ᵢ(Qᵢ) (equations (B.1)–(B.3)) have monotone functionals 𝒬ᵢ on (ℕ → {true, false}, ⊑); lfp(𝒬ᵢ) and gfp(𝒬ᵢ) exist (Proposition A.10) and may differ, e.g. lfp(𝒬₃) = ⊥ while gfp(𝒬₃) = ⊤.

projections.cs_theory: Induction corresponds to lfp and coinduction to gfp of the same functional.
projections.swe_architecture: Recursive definitions in code have two possible meanings; specify which one is intended.
projections.practical_debugging: A self-referential rule that 'proves itself' holds under gfp but not under lfp: check which reading the checker uses.
projections.cyber: Circular trust (A trusts B trusts A) is accepted under gfp and rejected under lfp.

concepts.title: Contractive functionals and unique fixed points
concepts.formal_summary: lfp(𝒬₀) = gfp(𝒬₀) relates to Banach's Fixed Point Theorem: 𝒬₀ is contractive because 𝒬₀(Q)(n) only calls Q on arguments smaller than n; 𝒬₁, 𝒬₂, 𝒬₃ are not.

projections.cs_theory: When every recursive reference strictly decreases along a well-founded order (such as (ℕ, <) for 𝒬₀), least and greatest fixed points coincide.
projections.swe_architecture: Recursion that always strictly descends along a well-founded measure makes the inductive/coinductive choice coincide.
projections.practical_debugging: If lfp and gfp differ, some rule refers to an argument that does not strictly decrease in a well-founded order: find it.
projections.cyber: Well-founded policy rules have a unique meaning; circular ones do not.

concepts.title: Inductive definition and proof by induction
concepts.formal_summary: For a monotone functional 𝒬, the inductive definition is Q = lfp(𝒬) (B.4), written as a rule system (B.5); when each rule has finitely many calls to Q both coincide with ⨆ₖ 𝒬ᵏ(⊥). Monotonicity of 𝒬 is assumed (a clause such as Q(Con₁(d)) iff ¬Q(d) is not acceptable).

projections.cs_theory: Semantics and derivation systems are inductive: only what can be derived holds.
projections.swe_architecture: Rule systems with finitary premises can be evaluated bottom-up to their least model.
projections.practical_debugging: A negated recursive premise breaks monotonicity; the rule system then has no lfp guarantee.
projections.cyber: Least-privilege authorisation [external] is an inductive definition: grant only what is derivable.

conditions: Monotone predicate functional 𝒬 on complete lattice (D → {true, false}, ⊑); rule form (B.5) agrees with Q = lfp(𝒬) when each rule makes finitely many recursive calls to Q
differs: Proposition A.10 characterises lfp(𝒬) = ⨅Red(𝒬) order-theoretically, whereas Appendix B presents inductive definitions as finitary inference rules (B.5) proved by rule-validity induction

concepts.title: Coinductive definition and proof by coinduction
concepts.formal_summary: Q = gfp(𝒬); proof rule Q′ ⊑ 𝒬(Q′) ⟹ Q′ ⊑ Q (from gfp(𝒬) = ⨆Ext(𝒬)); derived rule Q′ ⊑ 𝒬(Q ⊔ Q′) ⟹ Q′ ⊑ Q.

projections.cs_theory: Coinduction proves membership in greatest fixed points, e.g. acceptability in Chapter 3.
projections.swe_architecture: Checkers for cyclic structures (recursive types, infinite behaviours) assume consistency until violated.
projections.practical_debugging: If a coinductive check accepts too much, look for trivial self-justifying rules.
projections.cyber: Coinductive acceptance is optimistic; it must not be used where least privilege [external] is required.

conditions: Monotone predicate functional 𝒬 on complete lattice (D → {true, false}, ⊑) with coinductive specification Q = gfp(𝒬)
differs: Proposition A.10 gives the lattice identity gfp(𝒬) = ⨆Ext(𝒬), whereas §B.3 packages witness membership Q′ ∈ Ext(𝒬) (Q′ ⊑ 𝒬(Q′) or Q′ ⊑ 𝒬(Q ⊔ Q′)) as the coinduction proof principle

concepts.title: Example B.1: coinduction for mutually defined relations
concepts.formal_summary: For (R₁, R₂) = gfp(ℛ) with monotone ℛ = (ℛ₁, ℛ₂): from R₁′ ⊑ ℛ₁(R₁′, R₂′) and R₂′ ⊑ ℛ₂(R₁′, R₂′) conclude R₁′ ⊑ R₁ and R₂′ ⊑ R₂ (with a work-saving variant using R ⊔ R′).

projections.cs_theory: Coinduction extends componentwise to systems of relations.
projections.swe_architecture: Mutually recursive checks can share one coinductive hypothesis set.
projections.practical_debugging: When mutual coinductive checks disagree, verify both components of the candidate relation are extensive ((R₁′, R₂′) ∈ Ext(ℛ), i.e. Rᵢ′ ⊑ ℛᵢ(R₁′, R₂′)).
projections.cyber: Bisimulation-style [external] equivalence checks are mutual coinductive relations.

concepts.title: Example B.2: inductive vs coinductive reading of a grammar
concepts.formal_summary: For S → 0 | 1 | 0S | 1S over {0,1,2}^∞: inductively S = {0,1}⁺; coinductively S = {0,1}⁺ ∪ {0,1}^ω. Adding S → S leaves the inductive reading unchanged but makes the coinductive reading all of {0,1,2}^∞.

projections.cs_theory: Rule sets equivalent under induction can differ under coinduction.
projections.swe_architecture: Adding an innocuous-looking identity rule can change the meaning of a coinductive specification.
projections.practical_debugging: A coinductive checker that suddenly accepts everything probably gained a trivial self-rule.
projections.cyber: Self-referential policy rules (x allowed if x allowed) open everything under gfp.

concepts.title: Directed graphs, paths and cycles
concepts.formal_summary: G = (N, A) with N finite and A ⊆ N × N; paths as edge or node sequences (the trivial path has length 0); paths•(n, n′) and cycles(n) = {p ∈ paths•(n, n) | p ≠ [n]}; flow graphs (Example C.1) and FUN constraint graphs (Example C.2) are digraphs.

projections.cs_theory: Common substrate for flow graphs (Chapter 2) and constraint graphs (Chapter 3).
projections.swe_architecture: Represent CFGs and constraint graphs with the same graph abstraction to reuse algorithms.
projections.practical_debugging: The model excludes parallel edges and infinite node sets; real CFGs with multi-edges need normalisation.
projections.cyber: Control-flow and data-dependence graphs are the substrate of path-based vulnerability queries.

concepts.title: Acyclic graphs, DAGs and topological sorts
concepts.formal_summary: G is acyclic iff cycles(n) = ∅ for all n (a DAG); a topological sort orders nodes with n before n′ for every edge (n, n′); a digraph has a topological sort iff it is acyclic. A multiple-entry cycle has two distinct nodes entered from outside the cycle.

projections.cs_theory: Acyclic graphs admit one-pass propagation in topological order.
projections.swe_architecture: Dependency and build graphs are processed in topological order; cycles need special handling.
projections.practical_debugging: A topological sort failure is a cycle detector.
projections.cyber: Multiple-entry cycles are a hallmark of irreducible, possibly obfuscated [external] control flow.

concepts.title: Strong components and the reduced graph
concepts.formal_summary: 𝒮𝒞 = {(n, n′) | paths exist both ways} is an equivalence relation (Fact C.3); its classes are the strong components; the reduced graph has one node per component and no self-loops, and is a DAG (Lemma C.5). Example C.4: outermost loops of WHILE programs form strong components.

projections.cs_theory: Strong components isolate the cyclic parts of a constraint system (used in Section 6.3).
projections.swe_architecture: Solve components in topological order of the reduced graph; iterate only inside components.
projections.practical_debugging: Slow convergence localised to one component points to a long cycle inside it.
projections.cyber: Component-wise solving bounds analyser work on adversarial inputs [external].

concepts.title: Handles, roots and dummy roots
concepts.formal_summary: H ⊆ N is a handle if every node is reachable from some h ∈ H; r is a root iff {r} is a handle; a dummy root r ∉ N with edges to H makes any handle rooted; minimal handles exist since N is finite and are singletons iff the graph is rooted. init(S) is a root of the forward flow graph; final(S) is a handle of the backward flow graph (Example C.6).

projections.cs_theory: Iteration starts from a handle; backward analyses start from final labels.
projections.swe_architecture: Add a synthetic entry node when a graph has several entry points.
projections.practical_debugging: Nodes unreachable from the handle receive no information: check the handle covers all entries.
projections.cyber: Missing entry points (callbacks, handlers) leave code unanalysed.

concepts.title: Forests, trees, parents, ancestors and ordered forests
concepts.formal_summary: A forest is a DAG whose nodes have in-degree at most 1; a tree is a forest with a root; parent/child, ancestor/descendant (reflexive transitive closures), proper variants; ordered forests linearly order the children of each node.

projections.cs_theory: Spanning forests underlie edge classification and reverse postorder.
projections.swe_architecture: DFS trees are the data structure behind loop detection.
projections.practical_debugging: Ancestor tests decide back edges; get the reflexive closure right for self-loops.
projections.cyber: Tree-shaped call or ownership structures make dominance checks cheap.

concepts.title: Dominators
concepts.formal_summary: n′ dominates n if every path from H to n contains n′; Dom(n) is the greatest solution of Dom(n) = {n} if n ∈ H, Dom(n) = {n} ∪ ⋂{Dom(n′) | (n′, n) ∈ A} otherwise; proper and direct dominance defined from it.

projections.cs_theory: A greatest-fixed-point graph problem; the least solution of the same equation is wrong on cyclic graphs.
projections.swe_architecture: Dominator computation is a must-analysis over the flow graph.
projections.practical_debugging: Too-small dominator sets usually mean the equation was solved from ⊥ instead of ⊤.
projections.cyber: A security check dominates a sink iff every path to the sink passes it.

concepts.title: Depth-first spanning forest (Table C.1)
concepts.formal_summary: Table C.1 builds a depth-first spanning forest T = (N, A_T) from a graph with handle H and numbers nodes in reverse postorder (i counts down from k); the DFSF is not unique because the choice of node is unspecified. The table writes 'choose a node h in H' where an unvisited h is intended.

projections.cs_theory: Source of the reverse-postorder numbering used by iteration strategies.
projections.swe_architecture: DFS from all handle nodes, numbering on exit, yields the iteration order for forward analyses.
projections.practical_debugging: Re-running DFS from an already visited handle node corrupts the numbering; choose only unvisited nodes.
projections.cyber: Different DFS choices give different forests; results relying on a particular forest are fragile.

concepts.title: Tree, forward, back and cross edges
concepts.formal_summary: Relative to a spanning forest: tree edges; forward edges (to a proper descendant); back edges (descendant to ancestor, including self-loops); cross edges (unrelated nodes), which Table C.1 makes go from later-visited (lower rPostorder) to earlier-visited (higher rPostorder) nodes. Example C.8: WHILE flow graphs have no forward edges.

projections.cs_theory: Back edges close cycles; they are where iteration must repeat.
projections.swe_architecture: Loop headers are back-edge targets; that is where widening belongs.
projections.practical_debugging: Back edges depend on the chosen forest unless the graph is reducible.
projections.cyber: Widening at back-edge targets keeps analyses of obfuscated code [external] terminating.

concepts.title: Reverse postorder and its properties
concepts.formal_summary: Lemma C.9: (n, n′) is a back edge iff rPostorder[n] ≥ rPostorder[n′] (self-loop iff equal). Corollary C.10: every cycle contains a back edge. Corollary C.11: rPostorder topologically sorts tree, forward and cross edges. Corollary C.14: on reducible graphs every cycle-free path from the handle increases in rPostorder. Preorder and breadth-first order do not sort cross edges.

projections.cs_theory: Reverse postorder is the iteration order behind the bounds of Section 6.2.
projections.swe_architecture: For Bit Vector Frameworks relative to DFSF T, visiting nodes in reverse postorder propagates forward information in one pass per back edge (at most d(G_S, T) + 3 iterations by Lemma 6.12); general monotone frameworks are not bounded by d(G_S, T) alone.
projections.practical_debugging: Iterating in arbitrary order costs extra passes; switch to reverse postorder first.
projections.cyber: Order choice changes analyser cost on adversarial graphs [external], not least-fixed-point results.

concepts.title: Loop connectedness d(G, T)
concepts.formal_summary: d(G, T) (written d(G) when T is clear) is the largest number of back edges on any cycle-free path of G, relative to a DFSF T produced by Table C.1; for Figure C.1, d(G) = 1.

projections.cs_theory: With DFSF T and reverse postorder from Table C.1, d(G_S, T) + 3 bounds Round Robin iterations for Bit Vector Framework instances (Lemma 6.12); general monotone frameworks are not bounded by d(G_S, T) alone.
projections.swe_architecture: For Bit Vector Frameworks scheduled in reverse postorder relative to DFSF T, deeply nested loops cost at most d(G_S, T) + 3 passes; non-bit-vector monotone domains depend on lattice height or widening.
projections.practical_debugging: Quote iteration bounds with d(G, T), the Bit Vector Framework hypothesis, and the counting convention; T matters for irreducible graphs.
projections.cyber: On Bit Vector Framework analyses using reverse postorder, crafted deep loop nesting increases passes linearly in d(G_S, T) [external].

concepts.title: Dominator-back edges and reducible graphs
concepts.formal_summary: (n₁, n₂) is a dominator-back edge if n₂ dominates n₁; G is reducible iff removing them leaves an acyclic graph that still has handle H. Lemma C.12: in a reducible graph, back edges are exactly the dominator-back edges. Figure C.3 is the simplest irreducible graph. Example C.13: flow graphs of uniquely labelled WHILE statements are reducible and d(G) equals the maximum loop nesting depth.

projections.cs_theory: Reducibility makes back edges and d(G) independent of the spanning forest.
projections.swe_architecture: Structured languages produce reducible graphs; goto-heavy or compiled code may not.
projections.practical_debugging: On irreducible graphs, loop headers are ill-defined; use DFSF back edges or strong components instead.
projections.cyber: Obfuscators [external] deliberately create irreducible multiple-entry cycles.

concepts.title: Regular expressions and their languages
concepts.formal_summary: Over a finite non-empty alphabet Σ: atomic Λ, ∅, a ∈ Σ; compound (R₁ + R₂), (R₁ · R₂), (R₁)*; ℒ⟦·⟧ maps them to languages (union, concatenation, iteration ⋃ₖ Lᵏ); R₁ = R₂ iff ℒ⟦R₁⟧ = ℒ⟦R₂⟧.

projections.cs_theory: Path sets of graphs can be described by regular expressions (used in Mini Project 1.1).
projections.swe_architecture: Path-expression summaries [external] compress sets of paths for repeated queries.
projections.practical_debugging: Distinguish Λ (empty string) from ∅ (empty language); OCR and hand transcription confuse them.
projections.cyber: Regular path queries describe allowed and forbidden call sequences.

concepts.title: Homomorphisms on regular expressions
concepts.formal_summary: h : Σ₁ → Σ₂* extends to words, languages and regular expressions (h(∅) = ∅, h(Λ) = Λ, h(R₁ + R₂) = h(R₁) + h(R₂), h(R₁ · R₂) = h(R₁) · h(R₂), h(R*) = h(R)*), and ℒ(h(R)) = h(ℒ(R)).

projections.cs_theory: Relabelling path expressions commutes with taking languages.
projections.swe_architecture: Abstracting events by a homomorphism preserves regular structure.
projections.practical_debugging: Erasing symbols (h(a) = Λ) can merge distinct behaviours; check the mapping before comparing languages.
projections.cyber: Projecting traces onto security-relevant events preserves regularity of the policy language.

concepts.title: Index of Notation and symbol-scope disambiguation
concepts.formal_summary: Three-part Index of Notation (pp. 429–432: special symbols, Greek letters, Latin/script identifiers) plus unindexed core symbols and typeface/scope collisions (such as italic vs sans Q, Σ state vs alphabet, ς store vs reduction, and ? uninitialised label vs alphabet symbol).

projections.cs_theory: Typeface (italic, sans-serif, bold, calligraphic) and chapter scope disambiguate overloaded formal symbols across the six chapters and appendices.
projections.swe_architecture: Centralise symbol-to-type/scope tables in ontology/notation_index.md rather than assuming global 1-to-1 symbol uniqueness.
projections.practical_debugging: Before treating two formulas with the same glyph as related, check ontology/notation_index.md for typeface or chapter-scope collisions (see BKL-024, BKL-035).
projections.cyber: Ambiguous symbol transcription (e.g. conflating ⊆ with ⊇ or ? sentinel labels with alphabet symbols) silently inverts soundness checks [external].

concepts.title: Safe approximation
concepts.formal_summary: Program analysis statically predicts safe and computable approximations to the set of values or behaviours arising at run time; since questions such as termination are undecidable, answers are approximate, erring on the safe side: the values are 'among' those predicted (Figure 1.1).

projections.cs_theory: Undecidability forces approximation; safety is containment of the true answer.
projections.swe_architecture: Every analysis result is an over-approximation contract; clients must tolerate spurious entries.
projections.practical_debugging: Distinguish imprecision (extra facts, still safe) from unsoundness (missing facts).
projections.cyber: Sound bug-absence claims require over-approximation; exploit witnesses are under-approximations [external].

concepts.title: Semantics based (not semantics directed) analysis
concepts.formal_summary: The book advocates semantics-based analysis, whose results are provably safe with respect to a semantics, and does not cover semantics-directed analysis, whose structure merely mirrors a semantics.

projections.cs_theory: Correctness is a theorem relating analysis and semantics, not a structural resemblance.
projections.swe_architecture: Keep a reference semantics alongside an analysis so soundness can be stated and tested.
projections.practical_debugging: An analysis 'derived from' an interpreter is not thereby proven safe.
projections.cyber: Security claims need a stated semantics against which the analysis is proven safe.

concepts.title: Four approaches to program analysis
concepts.formal_summary: The book presents Data Flow Analysis, Constraint Based (Control Flow) Analysis, Abstract Interpretation and Type and Effect Systems, illustrated in Chapter 1 on common examples; they share a backbone of least solutions to equations or constraints.

projections.cs_theory: Different formalisms for the same goal: safe approximation via least fixed points.
projections.swe_architecture: Pick the formalism that matches the program representation available (flow graph, terms, semantics, types).
projections.practical_debugging: When two approaches disagree on a result, compare their least solutions, not arbitrary solutions.
projections.cyber: Security tooling mixes the approaches (data flow for taint, CFA for call targets, types for capabilities) [external].

concepts.title: WHILE language, labels and elementary blocks
concepts.formal_summary: Programs are WHILE statements whose elementary blocks (assignments, skip, tests) carry labels; distinct blocks are assumed to carry distinct labels; abstract syntax is used, concrete syntax is out of scope.

projections.cs_theory: Labels are the program points to which analysis information is attached.
projections.swe_architecture: An IR for analysis needs stable, unique block identifiers.
projections.practical_debugging: Duplicate labels silently merge facts of different blocks and make analyses less accurate.
projections.cyber: Code locations in findings must map back to unique labels.

concepts.title: Reaching Definitions
concepts.formal_summary: An assignment [x := a]^ℓ may reach a program point if there is an execution where x was last assigned at ℓ when that point is reached; uninitialised variables carry the special label ?; adding pairs keeps an analysis safe, removing a needed pair makes it unsafe (Table 1.1).

projections.cs_theory: A may-analysis: larger sets are safe.
projections.swe_architecture: The canonical example for def-use infrastructure and slicing.
projections.practical_debugging: A definition missing from the result is a soundness bug; an extra one is imprecision.
projections.cyber: Reaching uninitialised (?) facts flag possible uses of uninitialised data [external].

concepts.title: Equational formulation of Reaching Definitions
concepts.formal_summary: Entry and exit equations RD_entry(ℓ), RD_exit(ℓ) over the flow graph (Figure 1.2) define a monotone F on (𝒫(Var⋆ × Lab⋆))²ᵇ — 12 components for the 6-block Example 1.1 factorial program; since this lattice is finite, Fⁿ(∅⃗) stabilises and is the least solution of RD⃗ = F(RD⃗). Kill sets range over all labels including ?.

projections.cs_theory: Least fixed point of a monotone function on a finite lattice, reached from ⊥.
projections.swe_architecture: Per-block transfer functions plus merge equations: the classic data-flow framework shape.
projections.practical_debugging: Starting from a non-bottom value or omitting ? from kill sets changes the result.
projections.cyber: Taint propagation equations follow the same entry/exit pattern [external].

conditions: Same monotone transfer operator F collected per left-hand side over finite complete lattice (𝒫(Var⋆ × Lab⋆))²ᵇ
differs: Inclusions RD⃗ ⊒ F(RD⃗) admit larger reductive non-fixed-point solutions outside Fix(F), whereas every equation solution solves the inclusions and both share the same least solution

concepts.title: Constraint-based formulation of Reaching Definitions
concepts.formal_summary: Replacing equations by inclusions RD⃗ ⊒ F(RD⃗) yields a constraint system where every equation solution solves the constraints (Fix(F) ⊆ Red(F)), larger non-fixed-point solutions may exist, and both systems share the same least solution. The printed control-flow constraint list on p. 9 omits RD_entry(4) ⊇ RD_exit(3), which the general rule and Figure 1.2 require (see BKL-025).

projections.cs_theory: Every fixed point of F solves both RD⃗ = F(RD⃗) and RD⃗ ⊒ F(RD⃗) (Fix(F) ⊆ Red(F)); inclusions admit extra reductive solutions, while both systems share the same least solution.
projections.swe_architecture: Constraint generation decouples program traversal from solving.
projections.practical_debugging: Never compare non-least solutions across the two formulations; derive constraints from the rule, not the printed list.
projections.cyber: Rule-based analysers (Datalog-style [external]) compute least models of inclusion constraints.

conditions: Same monotone transfer operator F collected per left-hand side over finite complete lattice (𝒫(Var⋆ × Lab⋆))²ᵇ
differs: Inclusions RD⃗ ⊒ F(RD⃗) admit larger reductive non-fixed-point solutions outside Fix(F), whereas every equation solution solves the inclusions and both share the same least solution

concepts.title: Control Flow Analysis by constraints (Chapter 1 preview)
concepts.formal_summary: For a simple functional language, an abstract cache Ĉ(ℓ) and environment ρ̂(x) record the abstractions that subexpressions and variables may evaluate to; abstractions, variables and conditional application constraints (e.g. {fn x => [x]^1} ⊆ Ĉ(2) ⇒ Ĉ(4) ⊆ ρ̂(x)) are generated from the syntax and their least solution is sought. Facts are attached to labels only because the language has no side effects.

projections.cs_theory: Same pattern as data flow constraints: syntax yields constraints, least solution desired.
projections.swe_architecture: Call-target resolution precedes data flow analysis in higher-order programs.
projections.practical_debugging: A function shown as never applied (empty ρ̂) may indicate dead code or a missing constraint.
projections.cyber: Resolving indirect calls bounds where attacker-controlled data can flow [external].

concepts.title: Collecting semantics over traces
concepts.formal_summary: Traces record assignments as (variable, label) pairs; SRD(tr) gives semantically reaching definitions; collecting-semantics equations CS_entry/CS_exit over 𝒫(Trace) have a least solution, which is not computable by finite iteration and ignores test outcomes (a superset of real traces).

projections.cs_theory: A concrete reference semantics against which analyses are proven correct.
projections.swe_architecture: Design analyses top-down from a semantics, then abstract.
projections.practical_debugging: The collecting semantics over-approximates real traces; correctness, not exactness, is inherited.
projections.cyber: Trace-based semantics underpin path-sensitive security reasoning [external].

concepts.title: Abstraction and concretisation (adjunction) and the induced analysis
concepts.formal_summary: α(X) = {(x, SRD(tr)(x)) | x ∈ DOM(tr) ∧ tr ∈ X} and γ(Y) = {tr | ∀x ∈ DOM(tr) : (x, SRD(tr)(x)) ∈ Y} satisfy α(X) ⊆ Y ⇔ X ⊆ γ(Y) (an adjunction, Figure 1.3); the induced analysis α⃗ ∘ G ∘ γ⃗ satisfies α⃗ ∘ G ∘ γ⃗ ⊑ F, so α⃗(lfp(G)) ⊑ lfp(α⃗ ∘ G ∘ γ⃗) ⊑ lfp(F); optimality is a separate question (Exercise 1.4).

projections.cs_theory: Calculating an analysis from a semantics guarantees correctness by construction.
projections.swe_architecture: Define abstraction and concretisation explicitly; derive transfer functions from them.
projections.practical_debugging: If α ∘ G ∘ γ is not below the hand-written F, the hand-written analysis is not justified by this route.
projections.cyber: γ(∅) still contains the empty trace, so induced transfer functions are not strict (see BKL-033).

concepts.title: Annotated base types for Reaching Definitions (Table 1.2)
concepts.formal_summary: Judgements S : RD₁ → RD₂ annotate the state type; the first reading as equalities fails on conditionals, the working reading uses inclusions and a subsumption rule [sub], which brings the system close to the constraint-based formulation.

projections.cs_theory: Type systems can express data flow facts; subsumption plays the role of inclusion.
projections.swe_architecture: Rule-based checkers need a subsumption rule to merge branches.
projections.practical_debugging: A type system without subsumption rejects valid programs at conditionals.
projections.cyber: Annotated types can carry security labels with subsumption as label weakening [external].

concepts.title: Annotated type constructors (Table 1.3)
concepts.formal_summary: Judgements S : Σ --X/RD--> Σ record the variables X definitely assigned and the reaching definitions RD produced by S; [if] intersects X sets but unions RD sets, [wh] uses ∅ for X because the body may not run; results describe what a statement produces, not entry facts.

projections.cs_theory: May and must information flow differently through the same rule system.
projections.swe_architecture: Compositional summaries describe the effect of a statement independent of its context.
projections.practical_debugging: Do not compare Table 1.3 results with entry facts of Table 1.1; they answer different questions.
projections.cyber: Must-assigned sets support definite-initialisation checks [external].

concepts.title: Call-tracking effect system (Table 1.4)
concepts.formal_summary: Judgements Γ ⊢ e : τ & φ annotate function types τ₁ --φ--> τ₂ with the latent effect φ (functions that may be called); [var] and [fn] have empty effects under call-by-value; [app] combines the operator, operand and latent effects.

projections.cs_theory: Effects record computational behaviour alongside types.
projections.swe_architecture: Effect annotations give modular summaries of which functions a call may invoke.
projections.practical_debugging: The empty effects of [var] and [fn] depend on call-by-value; other strategies change the rules.
projections.cyber: Latent effects can bound which capabilities a callee may exercise [external].

concepts.title: Chaotic iteration (Table 1.5)
concepts.formal_summary: Initialise all RD components to ∅ and, while some RD_j ≠ F_j(RD⃗), update RD_j := F_j(RD⃗); the invariant RD⃗ ⊑ F(RD⃗) (guaranteed by starting at ∅⃗) yields the least solution; it is the principle behind the algorithms of Chapters 2 and 6.

projections.cs_theory: Because Table 1.5 updates only components with RD_j ≠ F_j(RD⃗) starting from ∅⃗, every step strictly enlarges RD⃗ and any valid update choice reaches the least fixed point on a finite lattice (fairness is needed only in unguarded chaotic-iteration schedules that permit no-op updates [external]).
projections.swe_architecture: Worklist solvers are chaotic iteration with a scheduling policy.
projections.practical_debugging: Results that depend on update order indicate a non-monotone transfer function or a non-bottom start.
projections.cyber: Solver order affects cost, not results, so adversarial inputs target cost [external].

concepts.title: Constant Folding transformation (Table 1.6)
concepts.formal_summary: RD ⊢ S ▷ S′ rewrites assignments using Reaching Definitions ([ass₁] substitutes a constant when all reaching definitions of y assign the same numeral and (y, ?) does not reach; [ass₂] evaluates closed expressions); ▷ is one step, neither reflexive nor transitive, with no fixed order; re-using RD after folding is valid because folding changes nothing RD observes.

projections.cs_theory: Analysis results justify transformations; validity after rewriting is a separate question.
projections.swe_architecture: Pass pipelines must state which analyses a rewrite preserves.
projections.practical_debugging: Re-using stale analysis results after label- or flow-changing rewrites is unsafe.
projections.cyber: Semantics-preserving rewrites can still remove security-relevant code (see BKL-032).

concepts.title: Mini Project 1.1: correctness of Reaching Definitions via regular expressions
concepts.formal_summary: Program paths are described by a regular expression 𝒮(S) over a label alphabet, and correctness conditions for the X and RD components of Table 1.3 are stated with homomorphisms h_y on the language ℒ⟦𝒮(S)⟧; proofs use the induction principles of Appendix B and the regular-expression material of Appendix C.

projections.cs_theory: Connects type-based summaries to path languages.
projections.swe_architecture: Path expressions [external] give a declarative specification of data flow facts.
projections.practical_debugging: The p. 30 X-condition applies h_y twice (see BKL-027); follow the p. 31 RD form.
projections.cyber: Regular path conditions express 'no redefinition on any path' properties [external].

concepts.title: WHILE control-flow extraction, label consistency, and boundary isolation
concepts.formal_summary: Syntax-directed CFG maps init: Stmt→Lab, final: Stmt→𝒫(Lab), blocks, labels, flow, and reversed flow^R over WHILE; AExp⋆ keeps non-trivial arithmetic subexpressions only. Assumes label consistency ([B₁]^ℓ,[B₂]^ℓ∈blocks(S) ⇒ B₁=B₂) plus isolated entries/exits for §2.1 equational schemas.
conditions: Label consistency (implied by unique labelling) makes [B]^ℓ ∈ blocks(S⋆) unambiguous.
Program-of-interest restriction Lab⋆, Var⋆, AExp⋆ (non-trivial only) enforces finiteness for ACC.
Isolated exits fails whenever S⋆ ends in a while-loop (Example 2.3 power program).
Single-block statements cannot drop {init(S)} or final(S) in the labels(S) graph identity.

projections.cs_theory: Gives every statement a rooted finite transition system invariant modulo syntactic branch guards.
projections.swe_architecture: Enforce label consistency as an IR invariant and separate AST CFG builders from solvers.
projections.practical_debugging: Trailing-loop failures trace to violated isolated-exits; variable noise in AE/VB indicates missing AExp⋆ non-trivial filtering.
projections.cyber: Syntactic flow ignores non-terminating loops, letting backward must-checks assume post-loop cleanup runs past infinite-loop DoS paths [external].

concepts.title: Available Expressions Analysis (Table 2.1)
concepts.formal_summary: Forward must-analysis (⋂, →, ↑) over (𝒫(AExp⋆), ⊇) determining which non-trivial expressions must have been evaluated and not modified along every path to ℓ; kill_AE([x:=a]^ℓ) removes a' mentioning x and gen_AE([x:=a]^ℓ) keeps {a' ∈ AExp(a) | x ∉ FV(a')}.
conditions: Largest solution under ⊆ (least under ⊇, ⊥_L = AExp⋆, ⋂∅ = AExp⋆); boundary AE_entry(init(S⋆)) = ∅.
Label consistent S⋆ and isolated entries required by Table 2.1 case-split equations.
gen_AE excludes x ∈ FV(a') because assignment overwrites x after evaluating RHS a.

projections.cs_theory: Dual to may-reachability: self-looping equations like X = {x+y} ∩ X require greatest fixed point under ⊆.
projections.swe_architecture: Drives common subexpression elimination [external] when non-extremal nodes initialise to AExp⋆.
projections.practical_debugging: Empty loop-header AE results diagnose initialising non-extremal nodes to ∅ instead of AExp⋆.
projections.cyber: Models mandatory validation checks before sensitive sinks where mutating checked bounds invalidates the guard (TOCTOU) [external].

concepts.title: Reaching Definitions Analysis in Chapter 2 (Table 2.2)
concepts.formal_summary: Forward may-analysis (⋃, →, ↓) over (𝒫(Var⋆ × Lab⋆^?), ⊆) with sentinel ? ∉ Lab⋆ tracking assignments (or uninitialised status) that may reach ℓ; RD_entry(init(S⋆)) = {(x, ?) | x ∈ FV(S⋆)} and kill_RD kills {(x, ?)} plus all assignments to x in S⋆.
conditions: Setting ι = ∅ instead of {(x, ?)} is unsound whenever read-before-write paths exist (§2.1.2).
Smallest solution under ⊆ (⊥_L = ∅, ⋃∅ = ∅).
Label consistency and isolated entries (unless §2.3 ι^ℓ_E join is used).

projections.cs_theory: Separates ? outside Lab⋆ (fixing Chapter 1's Lab⋆ inclusion) to totalise initial read-before-write traces.
projections.swe_architecture: Upstream producer for UD/DU chain indexes and Constant Folding.
projections.practical_debugging: Mis-folding an uninitialised variable usually stems from setting RD_entry(init(S⋆)) = ∅.
projections.cyber: Direct taint-reachability pattern and uninitialised-variable oracle ((x, ?) ∈ RD_entry(ℓ)) [external].

concepts.title: Very Busy Expressions Analysis (Table 2.3)
concepts.formal_summary: Backward must-analysis (⋂, ←, ↑) over (𝒫(AExp⋆), ⊇) along flow^R identifying expressions guaranteed to be evaluated before redefinition of any variable on all paths exiting ℓ; critically gen_VB([x:=a]^ℓ) = AExp(a) retains x-containing expressions.
conditions: Largest solution under ⊆ (⊥_L = AExp⋆); boundary VB_exit(ℓ) = ∅ on ℓ ∈ final(S⋆).
Label consistent S⋆ and isolated exits required by Table 2.3 case-split.
Code hoisting requires error-free / trap-free expression semantics (BKL-001).

projections.cs_theory: Backward dual of Available Expressions differing asymmetrically in gen_VB because RHS precedes LHS update.
projections.swe_architecture: Supports code-size hoisting when faults and loop divergence cannot trap.
projections.practical_debugging: Copying gen_AE's x ∉ FV(a') filter breaks self-updates like [x:=x+1]; trailing loops fail without isolated exits.
projections.cyber: Models mandatory cleanup obligations (zeroize/unlock) on all exit paths, modulo non-terminating loops [external].

concepts.title: Live Variables Analysis (Table 2.4) and Strongly Live Extension
concepts.formal_summary: Backward may-analysis (⋃, ←, ↓) over (𝒫(Var⋆), ⊆) tracking variables that may be read before redefinition on some exit path (kill_LV={x}, gen_LV=FV(a)); Exercise 2.4 refines to faint / strongly live variables by gating FV(a) on x ∈ l.
conditions: Smallest solution under ⊆; Table 2.4 assumes LV_exit(final) = ∅ unless output variables are observed.
Label consistent S⋆ and isolated exits (or §2.3 unconditional ι^ℓ_E join).
Strongly live variables stays distributive yet leaves Bit Vector Frameworks (Exercise 2.4/2.9).

projections.cs_theory: Dualises Dead Code Elimination safety: only variables outside over-approximated live sets are safely dead.
projections.swe_architecture: Parameterise final live set ι by escaped/output variables before dead-store removal.
projections.practical_debugging: Running Table 2.4 on trailing while-loops marks loop-carried writes spuriously dead.
projections.cyber: LV_exit(final)=∅ explains why compiler DCE deletes trailing secret zeroization stores (CWE-14, BKL-006) [external].

concepts.title: Use-Definition / Definition-Use Chains (Figure 2.23), Slicing, and SSA Form
concepts.formal_summary: Definition-clear path predicate clear(x, ℓ, ℓ') checks ¬def(x, ℓ_i) on 1..n-1 and use(x, ℓ_n), defining symmetric ud(x, ℓ') and du(x, ℓ); constructive UD(x, ℓ) reads RD_entry(ℓ) when x ∈ gen_LV(B^ℓ), whereas SSA ([U2b:CR-d]) inserts ϕ-nodes to make du-chains explicit.
conditions: Signature domain/codomain must include ? (Var⋆ × Lab⋆^? ↔ 𝒫(Lab⋆^?), fixing pp. 53–54 erratum).
Constant replacement at use ℓ' along du from [x:=n]^ℓ requires ALL defs in ud(x, ℓ') to assign constant n (Mini Project 2.1).
Explicit data chains omit control-dependence edges across branches unless augmented [external].

projections.cs_theory: ud and du are mutually transpose graph reachability relations over definition-clear CFG paths.
